<SUMMARY>The period of March 26 to April 2, 2026, was dominated by escalating geopolitical tensions in West Asia, particularly the ongoing conflict involving Iran, which triggered significant economic and supply chain disruptions globally. United States President Donald Trump issued repeated threats to Iran's energy and water infrastructure while also extending pauses on direct attacks. These tensions led to surging oil prices, impacts on Asian manufacturing, and critical shortages in materials like helium for the semiconductor industry. Concurrently, the global technology sector experienced dynamic shifts, with major AI-related investments and market competition, alongside persistent concerns over supply chain resilience and export controls. Developments in semiconductor manufacturing saw substantial investments in new fabs and advancements in lithography, while critical mineral supply chains witnessed strategic acquisitions and regional resource nationalism.</SUMMARY>
<EWS>The escalating conflict in West Asia, marked by Iran's threat to US tech firms and actual attacks on an oil tanker off Dubai, alongside reported power outages in Iran following infrastructure attacks, presents immediate risks of broader regional destabilization and increased energy market volatility. The continued disruption of global helium supplies due to the Iran war poses a critical threat to semiconductor manufacturing and healthcare sectors, with implications for AI chip production timelines. Persistent AI source code leaks from companies like Anthropic signal significant cybersecurity vulnerabilities within advanced technology firms. China's growing self-sufficiency in AI chip production, coupled with calls for boycotts of US conferences over sanctions, indicates a widening technological and geopolitical rift.</EWS>
<EXEC>
**Asia:**
Mitsui OSK Lines (MOL) and Hitachi agreed to develop a floating datacenter in Japan, targeting operations for 2027 or later. Nvidia's market share in China fell to 55% from a claimed high of 95%, as local chip makers delivered 1.65 million AI GPUs, capturing 41% of the Chinese AI semiconductor market. China urged a boycott of a top US conference over a sanctions ban, prompting the conference to apologize and reverse its policy on papers from US-sanctioned entities. Air Liquide inaugurated its first Advanced Materials manufacturing plant in Taiwan, aiming to strengthen the next-gen semiconductor supply chain. China's chip equipment and supply chain scaled up on AI demand. Nexchip applied for a Hong Kong listing amidst mature-node expansion. South Korea proposed over $17 billion in additional budget to ease energy costs due to the Iran war. Japanese opinion on military deployment in Iran is nudged by energy security concerns.

**Africa:**
Zimbabwe and Zambia pushed back against US health deals that requested health data and minerals. Zimbabwe disrupted China’s lithium flow with an export ban, impacting China’s battery supply chain. Chinese company Zijin is set to open one of the world’s biggest lithium mines in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Ghana's first lithium mine is set to export to the USA. A US firm, Virtus, acquired a Congolese cobalt miner, gaining clearance to restart Congo cobalt mines. The Congo regulator set an April 30 deadline for cobalt miners to use 2025 export quotas.

**Europe:**
Intel announced a $14.2 billion repurchase of its Ireland fab stake, which strengthens its balance sheet and supports the 18A process node launch, contributing to a 9% stock jump. SEMI projected worldwide 300 mm fab equipment spending to increase 18% to $133 billion in 2026 and 14% to $151 billion in 2027. A Microsoft-backed start-up secured $40 million for helium atom beam lithography. European Union (EU) energy ministers sought to coordinate a response to the Iran war, with the EU potentially reviving 2022 energy crisis measures. Chinese chip industry leaders admitted the country lags five to ten years behind in AI data center chips, noting strain on equipment and talent supply. Spain blocked US war flights over the Iran war.

**Americas:**
Microsoft and Chevron entered an exclusivity deal to power a West Texas AI data center complex with 2.5 gigawatts of power. AMD announced it would acquire Intel. Intel stock jumped 8% to $47.50, and AMD stock gained 3% near $209, driven by AI chip demand. Anthropic accidentally exposed the source code for its Claude Code, marking the second such incident in less than a week, leading to takedown requests. Oracle slashed thousands of jobs to fund its AI expansion. SpaceX filed confidentially for an IPO, potentially valued at $1.75 trillion, with plans to launch up to 1 million data-center satellites into orbit. NVIDIA submitted MLPerf Inference v6.0 benchmarks, showcasing Blackwell Ultra's dominance over competitors. Cognichip raised $60 million to develop AI-designed chips. The US-Ukrainian minerals deal, advocated by J.C. Ellis in 2025, aimed to ensure Ukrainian control and allied access to critical minerals. A federal judge in Nevada ruled against stopping the Rhyolite Ridge Lithium/Boron Mine Project. Greenland Resources signed an eight-year off-take agreement with SSAB to supply molybdenum. American Rare Earths accelerated a pilot plant to produce rare earth concentrate from Halleck Creek. Eagle Nuclear Energy announced a 27,000 ft drill program for its Aurora uranium deposit. Manna Air Delivery raised $50 million in Series B funding, planning US expansion. Three individuals were charged with attempting to break US sanctions on AI chips for China. A US judge suspended government sanctions on AI company Anthropic. GlobalFoundries committed $3 billion more to US fabs and filed patent lawsuits against Tower Semiconductor seeking an import ban. OmniVision invested $145 million in a wafer foundry. Samsung ramped up hiring as its Texas foundry neared wafer preparation. TSMC plans to build 12 fabs in Arizona. A bill to ban the sale of key AI chipmaking equipment to China was introduced in the House.

**Oceania:**
A US deep-sea mineral processing plant is planned by Glomar, with Australia's Cobalt Blue. Australia is expected to generate 90,000 tonnes of solar panel waste annually by 2030.

<CONCLUSION>The reporting period of March 26 - April 2, 2026, saw a continued and intense focus on the West Asia conflict, with significant ripple effects across global energy markets, supply chains, and technological development. President Trump's fluctuating rhetoric and actions regarding Iran, from extending pauses on attacks to issuing severe threats against energy and water infrastructure, maintained a high level of uncertainty. The conflict directly impacted energy prices, Asian manufacturing, and the critical helium supply, underscoring vulnerabilities in the global semiconductor industry. In the tech sector, AI development continued at pace with major investments and market shifts, but also highlighted security risks from data leaks and geopolitical competition, particularly between the US and China. Critical mineral supply chains emerged as key points of geopolitical leverage, with African nations asserting greater control and the US actively seeking to secure access through acquisitions and partnerships. Overall, the period was characterized by a complex interplay of escalating military tensions, economic vulnerabilities, and strategic technological competition across multiple regions.</CONCLUSION>

<FINAL_CONCLUSION>The ongoing West Asia conflict and its pervasive global impacts on energy and critical material supply chains will remain the primary geopolitical driver in the immediate future, exacerbating existing vulnerabilities in the technology sector. The increasing weaponization of technology, evidenced by AI's role in warfare and the strategic importance of semiconductor access, will continue to intensify the geopolitical competition between major powers. States will likely accelerate efforts toward supply chain localization and diversification, especially for critical minerals and advanced chips, as a direct response to these instabilities. Further AI development and deployment will be shaped by these geopolitical realities, balancing innovation with national security and supply chain resilience objectives.</FINAL_CONCLUSION>
